foods.name: Beef, lamb, pork and chicken, cooked through
foods.why: Cooked right through with no pink and clear juices, meat is a green light and a top iron hit. Get leftovers into the fridge fast, then reheat them steaming hot within a day.

foods.name: Steak, well done
foods.why: No pink for now, but a steak cooked all the way through is all yours. Well done still comes with chips, and the iron is doing you both a favour.

foods.name: Sausages, cooked through
foods.why: Cook a snag right through until there is no pink left and it is a green light. The Bunnings sausage sizzle lives to see another Saturday.

foods.name: Bacon, served hot
foods.why: Cooked in the pan and served hot, bacon is a yes. Heat is what handles any listeria, so eat it straight off the heat rather than cold from the fridge.

foods.name: Hot BBQ chicken, fresh from the shop
foods.why: Straight from the hot cabinet and still steaming, BBQ chook is a green light. Leftovers go into the fridge within 2 hours and get eaten within a day, reheated hot.

foods.name: Ham or salami, heated steaming hot
foods.why: Heat is the loophole. Deli meats taken right up to steaming hot, on a pizza or in a toastie, are back on the menu: listeria does not survive 74C for two minutes.

foods.name: Canned or jar meat and fish paste
foods.why: Shelf-stable tins and jars are safe as houses until you open them. After that, treat it like any fresh food: straight into the fridge and eaten up quickly.

foods.name: Liver
foods.why: Liver is an iron legend, but it is packed with retinol and too much vitamin A is not great for the bump. Keep it to 50g a week, about one small slice.
foods.makeItGreen: Stay under 50g a week, roughly one small slice, and cook it right through.
foods.swap: Red meat, chickpeas or leafy greens bring the iron with no vitamin A cap.

foods.name: Rare or medium-rare steak
foods.why: Pink in the middle can carry toxoplasmosis, so this one waits. The good news: a well-done steak is still very much a steak.
foods.makeItGreen: Order it well done, cooked right through with no pink left, and it is a green light.
foods.swap: A well-done scotch fillet with all the trimmings.

foods.name: Raw mince dishes (tartare, kibbeh)
foods.why: Raw mince has never met heat, so nothing has knocked out the bugs. Tartare and kibbeh are benched for the next few months.
foods.makeItGreen: Cook the mince right through until it is steaming: same flavours, safe version.
foods.swap: A rich slow-cooked bolognese, or a burger patty cooked all the way through.

foods.name: Cold deli meats
foods.why: Cold cured and cooked meats can carry listeria, and freshly sliced is not safer: the slicer itself can spread it around. Heat is what changes the answer.
foods.makeItGreen: Heat it until it is steaming hot right through, like on a pizza or in a toastie, and it is back on.
foods.swap: Tinned tuna, hot roast chicken, or firm-cooked egg in the sanga.

foods.name: Prosciutto
foods.why: Cured but never actually cooked, so cold prosciutto can carry listeria. Freshly sliced is not safer either, the slicer can pass it along.
foods.makeItGreen: Crisp it in a hot pan or under the grill until it sizzles, then scatter it over pasta or pizza.
foods.swap: Hot crispy prosciutto shards over pasta, or hot roast chicken in a sanga.

foods.name: Cold meats and chicken from sandwich shops and cafes
foods.why: Cold chicken and cold cuts at a sanga shop sit in the fridge and share a slicer and tongs, which is listeria's happy place.
foods.makeItGreen: Ask for it toasted until the filling is steaming hot right through.
foods.swap: A hot toasted sanga, or a salad you watched them make fresh.

foods.name: Cold leftover BBQ chicken
foods.why: Once cooked chicken has gone cold, listeria gets its chance. Straight from the fridge is a no, but it is only a reheat away from a yes.
foods.makeItGreen: Reheat it until it is steaming hot right through, and finish it within a day of buying it.
foods.swap: Hot chook fresh from the shop, or reheated chicken piled into a wrap.

foods.name: Pâté (refrigerated)
foods.why: Refrigerated pâté is a double whammy: listeria from a chilled ready-to-eat spread, plus a big hit of vitamin A from the liver.
foods.swap: Shelf-stable tinned or jar pâté (into the fridge once opened), or a home-made white bean dip.

foods.name: Veggie pâté (refrigerated)
foods.why: The refrigerated pâté rule is about the fridge, not the meat. Chilled ready-to-eat spreads can carry listeria, the veggie ones included.
foods.swap: A home-made white bean or beetroot dip, or a shelf-stable jar version.

foods.name: Jerky and biltong
foods.why: Jerky and biltong are dried and cured but never cooked, so nothing in there has been through heat. Sitting this one out for now.
foods.swap: Salted nuts, roasted chickpeas, or hot cooked meat straight off the barbie.
